Crypto blitzes midterms with $176 million to support allies as it prepares for post-Trump era

FILE PHOTO: U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks at the White House Crypto Summit at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., March 7, 2025. REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein

FAST

NEW YORK, Oct 27 : The crypto industry has spent roughly $176 million across more than 100 midterm races this election cycle, as part of a years-long plan to build a bipartisan coalition of allies in Congress that can advance its interests long after US President Donald Trump leaves office.  The $2.75 trillion industry, and the billionaires who built it, are aggressively spending to elect friendly candidates while targeting politicians they see as a threat, according to interviews with more than a half-dozen crypto political strategists and a Reuters review of the spending. While the industry’s recent spending blitz is known, its long-term plan to further its legislative agenda is less well-understood. The industry isn’t just looking for allies; it is trying to pick candidates who already have a chance of winning, and can help once they get to Congress, the strategists said.  Crypto's largest super political action committee, Fairshake, which spent $196 million during the 2024 election cycle, is leading the industry’s strategy again. Fairshake said 53 of the 58 candidates it supported in primaries or special elections this year won and will be on the ballot on November 3.

Super PACs can accept and spend unlimited sums of money, but cannot coordinate directly with campaigns. They are flooding several races with tens of millions of dollars in ads.  Voters have little way of knowing who pays for these ads, which barely mention crypto. Most of Fairshake's are sponsored by its affiliate PACs with innocuous names like "Defend American Jobs" and "Protect Progress." The ads often focus on hot-button issues like taxes or immigration. Perceived enemies, such as longtime skeptic Sherrod Brown, vying to return to the Senate in Ohio, can be subjected to an onslaught of often-personal attacks. Advocacy group Public Citizen said crypto was the single-biggest corporate spender in federal races in 2026, after saying in 2024 that its spending was "akin to a corporate Death Star hovering over elections."    The PACs' primary financiers, led by Coinbase, Ripple and venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, aren't trying to convince voters to support digital currencies. The money is a calling card to help forge long-term relationships with elected officials, said industry strategists, campaign staff, watchdog groups and political finance managers.  It underscores how the industry is behaving as other businesses do in Washington — using funds to open doors and buffer itself against regulation. The strategy reflects the reality that come 2029, the occupant of the White House is unlikely to be as personally invested in crypto as Trump, whose family made around $2.3 billion from crypto ventures between mid-2024 and April, a Reuters investigation found. “It's an investment in the future,” said Colin McLaren, head of government relations at crypto industry advocacy group the Solana Policy Institute, which has given $4.9 million to the midterms this year, according to campaign finance records.  The effort is designed to “ensure that over the next 100 years, the crypto industry has clear rules of the road, and that we know what our regulators are expecting from us," he said. Through October 20, Fairshake and its affiliate PACs have spent about $150.8 million on the midterms this year, while other crypto groups have spent around $25 million, according to campaign finance filings. "We back pro-crypto candidates who support American innovation in both parties, and look forward to continuing to build on the largest pro-crypto caucus in American history," said Geoff Vetter, spokesperson for Fairshake. COME A LONG WAY In 2018, lawmakers couldn’t even get a room in the House or Senate office buildings to hold the first congressional bipartisan roundtable discussion on crypto, instead meeting across the street from the US Capitol in the Library of Congress, said Kristin Smith, president of the Solana Policy Institute, who helped establish the Blockchain Association that year.  The Biden administration heavily scrutinized the industry following the collapse of FTX and an industry-wide meltdown in 2022, with the US Securities and Exchange Commission eventually levying more than $6 billion in penalties in 98 cases, according to a Georgetown University Law study.   “It was an all-out assault on the technology,” said Smith, the Blockchain Association's interim CEO. “The industry was in a corner, and the only way out was to show political force.”  Executives decided they needed a political strategy to combat what they called then-SEC chair Gary Gensler’s “regulation by enforcement,” lobbyists, advocacy groups and campaign strategists said. Coinbase Chief Policy Officer Faryar Shirzad was the architect behind nonprofit political advocacy group Stand With Crypto — which isn't required to disclose its donors — and Fairshake, which both launched in 2023. The number of Congresspeople with an "A" rating from Stand With Crypto is up to 332, compared with 96 when the group launched.   As the industry has won more legal clarity in Washington, its market value has nearly tripled from around $1 trillion in 2023 to about $2.75 trillion now, according to CoinGecko.  The combination of Trump, a growing bipartisan congressional coalition and a neutered opposition allowed the industry to advance its legislative agenda more in the last two years than some industries have done in decades, other industry lobbyists say. That includes 2025's Genius Act legislation establishing the first-ever US federal regulatory framework for stablecoins, enacted with overwhelming bipartisan support. That followed a White House meeting earlier in the year when industry leaders, including Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong and Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse, sat with Trump when the president declared an end to the "war on crypto."  "Moving that quickly in Washington is like light speed in space," said Ron Bonjean, partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions, and a former senior Senate aide.  The industry's real goal is passing the Clarity Act, which would put crypto oversight under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. That bill stalled in this congressional session and faces an uphill battle next year if Democrats win control of one or more chambers of Congress.  Without it, agency-level regulations undertaken during Trump's term can be reversed by a subsequent administration, analysts at JPMorgan said. Fairshake is financing House candidates from both parties, but it decided to only back Republicans in Senate races after Democrats in that chamber blocked the Clarity Act from advancing to a final vote. Their opposition centered around an ethics provision that would have forced the Trump family to sell their crypto holdings. Gary Kalman, of anti-corruption nonprofit Transparency International, criticized the bill for shifting regulation to the less-stringent CFTC, and for preempting states from enacting tougher laws. Coinbase and Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. Ripple didn't return requests for comment.  THE PRIME TARGET Fairshake's highest-profile win in 2024 was defeating Brown, an industry foe who chaired the Senate Banking Committee from 2021 to 2024.  Spending millions attacking the sitting chairman of the industry's oversight committee was unprecedented in Washington, corporate watchdogs and political strategists say. But the gamble paid off.  Now, Brown is running again, with public opinion polls showing him with a narrow lead over his opponent, Republican Jon Husted. The industry has spent more than $68 million on the race, helping to make it one of the most expensive on record, according to AdImpact. Fairshake’s ads opposing Brown, which it did not comment on, don't mention crypto. One charges him with voting to raise gas taxes in Ohio and raises a Reuters-debunked claim that he voted to "unleash 87,000 IRS agents on you while voting to give social security benefits to illegals."  “Of course, the special interests are panicking, they know Sherrod will fight the rigged system they're feasting on to stand up for working Ohioans,” said Patrick Eisenhauer, Brown's campaign manager.  A CRYPTO MONEY BOMB  In some races, crypto spending dwarfed candidate fundraising. The industry spent $5.3 million in a Maryland House Democratic primary to support state Delegate Adrian Boafo, who raised $1.9 million on his own, records show. Other non-crypto groups spent $6.8 million to support Boafo's campaign, which declined to comment.  “There were so many ads ... that it makes other candidates suffocate,” said Quincy Bareebe, a healthcare entrepreneur who came in second of 24 candidates in that primary despite spending $6.6 million of her own money. "Adrian was everywhere."  The industry was less successful in Illinois. Fairshake spent over $10.1 million on ads attacking Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton, who is running for US Senate, and another $2.5 million against Illinois state Representative La Shawn Ford, who is running for a Chicago-area congressional district. Both are expected to win on November 3. Ford defeated a dozen primary challengers despite raising just $500,000 and lending his campaign $175,000 to fight off industry-funded ads that brought up a 14-year-old federal indictment that was later dropped. His campaign issued a cease-and-desist letter to Fairshake, accusing it of making defamatory statements about him in its ads. Fairshake did not comment on its ads or Ford's response. Ford thinks Fairshake targeted him because he supported state legislation to require crypto exchanges and related companies to register with Illinois. “They were relentless, on every outlet, radio, TV, social media, mailers," Ford said. “It was personal and it was hurtful, and unnecessary for my family to have to go through.”

Source: Reuters

FAST

Oct 27 : Wall Street expects Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet to report on Wednesday faster growth in their cloud businesses, but a turbulent market selloff and concerns over rising costs of AI financing are tempering optimism. Investors are pressing for evidence that the AI boom can deliver swift returns to justify its enormous price tag. Rising bond yields at AI cloud providers such as CoreWeave and record costs to insure Meta Platform's debt have amplified concerns about how the massive AI infrastructure buildout is being funded, particularly as higher US interest rates loom. Market turmoil has rekindled warnings of an AI bubble from investors, including hedge fund Citadel's founder Ken Griffin, and pushed companies to delay their IPOs. An expected Democratic sweep of the US midterm elections could spell more trouble for data centers that are already a target of protests over their impact on power grids, electricity bills and the environment. Big Tech's results this week will be a litmus test for AI adoption and economic viability. These three companies — with nearly $1.7 trillion in combined backlog — plan to spend as much as $600 billion this year.

Meta's results last week showed just how unforgiving the calculus has become. Better-than-expected revenue growth and an upbeat outlook were overshadowed by increased spending plans, sending its shares down nearly 7 per cent the following day. They are now down more than 4 per cent this year. "The appetite for capital expenditure alone is slowing rapidly," said Brian Mulberry, chief market strategist at Zacks Investment Management. "For Amazon, Google and Microsoft specifically the growth in their cloud companies is a very important line item that will signal if further growth in capital expenditure can be funded without further risks of contracting free cash flow." While the trio's stocks have outperformed ad-driven Meta this year, with gains ranging from 1.2 per cent to 10.1 per cent, they continue to lag behind the S&P 500's near 12 per cent rise. Google Cloud is expected to again lead the three major players in the September quarter, with revenue surging 95.1 per cent to $29.57 billion, according to LSEG data. That would be faster than the 81.8 per cent growth in the previous quarter. Amazon Web Services, the market leader in cloud, is expected to post 38.2 per cent revenue growth, up from 36.8 per cent in the previous quarter. Microsoft Azure is expected to expand 47.7 per cent, accelerating from 42 per cent three months earlier, according to Visible Alpha data. Alphabet and Amazon are expected to burn cash for the second and third consecutive quarters, respectively, while Microsoft will likely generate more than $8 billion in cash flow. GOOGLE CLOUD SUCCESS, SEARCH CONCERNS Alphabet's cloud business and in-house chips have emerged as a bright spot in its AI push amid concerns Google's models are falling behind those of OpenAI and Anthropic. But competition from personal AI agents such as Meta's Muse as well as chatbots such as ChatGPT has raised concerns about the search business that has long powered its earnings. Google search revenue growth is expected to slow to 14.7 per cent from 16.8 per cent in the previous quarter, even as total revenue is expected to rise at a slightly faster pace of 25.2 per cent to $128.18 billion. "This quarter, we believe commentary is equally important to quantitative results as competition for search is growing again with agents while there is increased consternation around the payback of AI capital expenditure," Citizens analyst Andrew Boone said. MICROSOFT CHANGES REPORTING SEGMENTS Microsoft will report under a revamped structure for the first time on Wednesday, combining cloud, AI and business software into a division called "Agents and Infra", and Windows, gaming and ad sales into another dubbed "Devices and Consumer". A notable change will be the disclosure of Azure's quarterly revenue, resolving investor frustration over its previous focus on growth rates without absolute figures. Analysts expect Azure to post sales of $33.06 billion in the quarter, powering a 16.7 per cent rise in Microsoft's total revenue to $90.66 billion, slightly slower growth than the previous period. Amazon's overall revenue growth is expected to slow to 12.3 per cent from 19.6 per cent in the previous quarter.

Source: Reuters

FAST

Oct 27 : European shares slipped on Tuesday, dragged down by banking stocks, after disappointing results from HSBC, while investors also turned cautious ahead of US tech earnings, seen as a key test of the AI trade, and central bank meetings that could shape near-term interest-rate outlook. The STOXX 600 banking sector slid 1.3 per cent, with shares of Europe's largest lender down 7 per cent after missing revenue expectations for the July-September quarter due to slower growth at its wealth business, while pretax profit was in line with estimates. The pan-European STOXX 600 dipped 0.2 per cent, while London's FTSE 100 index declined 1 per cent, largely as a result of the drop in HSBC shares.   "Banks have been the winners of the latest quarter before this one, reporting record results because of high volatility and because of AI financing," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior market analyst at Swissquote Bank.

"But right now, they are coming under pressure because we do see the interest rate rise, short-term yields rising more than long-term; that's basically eating into the income revenue," she added. "But I still think that the banks are in a good position to outperform the other sectors, especially sectors that are more vulnerable to directly rising living costs." Quarterly earnings are the central focus globally, as investors weigh up the impact of the conflict in Iran, including higher costs and interest rates, on corporate performance. EARNINGS DELUGE In the US this week, more than a third of S&P 500 companies are expected to report and the scrutiny of AI hyperscalers including Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet will be intense, as investors seek signs that these companies' billion-dollar investments are yielding returns as expected. "We remain medium-term bullish on the 'picks and shovels' trade. We see capex cycle remaining strong and the earnings remaining robust," Mohit Kumar, an economist at Jefferies, said. "However, we do admit that, as with any cycle, there would be winners and losers in the AI trade and a number of companies will not remain profitable and even go bust." Big Tech earnings could determine appetite for the eagerly awaited public debut of AI bellwether Anthropic and Meta Platforms' $95-billion equity fundraising. Claude-owner Anthropic disclosed a steep loss, but red-hot revenue growth, in its filing for a US initial public offering on Monday and is expected to list before the end of November.   The enthusiasm around Anthropic lifted stocks in Asia and helped MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan rise 0.1 per cent. Nasdaq futures were muted after strong gains in the previous session. CENTRAL BANKS EXPECTED TO STAY ON HOLD Policy decisions from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan are due later this week, with economists expecting all three to stand pat on interest rates, leaving the focus on comments from policymakers to gauge the rates outlook. Fed policymakers have telegraphed they will not raise short-term borrowing costs again on Wednesday, but with inflation concerns still front and centre, investors believe a rate-hike pause will not last for long. Traders are pricing in a 25 basis point hike from the Fed in December, the CME Group's FedWatch Tool showed. The euro eased 0.1 per cent and at $1.115 it was near the May low it hit two weeks ago. The yield on the US 10-year Treasury note was steady at 4.986 per cent, staying below 5 per cent which it breached in September as investors scurried to Treasuries for safety during stock market tumult over AI worries.  The outlook for interest rates could depend on the outcome of ongoing talks with Tehran, even as Yemen's Houthis continue to attack Saudi Arabia. Brent crude prices rose 0.6 per cent to $116.82 per barrel.  Spot gold prices eased 0.6 per cent to $3,992.70 per ounce.

Source: Reuters

FAST

MOSCOW/LONDON, Oct 27 - OPEC+ oil-producing countries are likely to keep their December oil output targets steady on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year. The online meeting of seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — comes as Gulf members have been boosting exports that have been disrupted for months by the Iran war. Most, however, are still pumping well below their output targets. All three people declined to be named and said no final decision had been made. OPEC+ comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia. OPEC and authorities in Russia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In September, OPEC+ completed the phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023. Disruption caused by the Iran war has meant Gulf producers are falling below their quotas. Reuters reported in July that OPEC+ was likely to make no changes to its targets during the fourth quarter as it turns its focus to 2027 quota negotiations.  The group still has one more layer of production cuts of about 2 million bpd covering most members through the end of 2026. OPEC+ needs to finalise a review of members' production capacity before setting the 2027 baselines that will determine future quotas and shape plans to unwind those cuts, sources have said.

FAST

LONDON Oct 27 : The dollar nudged higher on the euro, yen and pound on Tuesday, as traders braced for a barrage of major central bank meetings that will shape the interest rate outlook, as well as key corporate earnings that could ripple through all asset classes. The Federal Reserve is set to announce its latest policy decision on Wednesday, the European Central Bank is up on Thursday, and the Bank of Japan rounds out the week on Friday. All three are expected to keep rates on hold, so the focus will be on any hints policymakers give on their outlook. Also helping the dollar, especially on safe havens like the yen and Swiss franc, was greater calm in the equity market which was roiled last week by renewed worries about high-flying AI stocks.

"The dollar has found good support early this week, as stabilising AI-related sentiment has allowed markets to reconnect with the broader supportive backdrop of a hawkish Federal Reserve and high energy prices," said Francesco Pesole, currency analyst at ING. The US currency was up 0.16 per cent on the yen at 157.73, while the euro slid 0.17 per cent to $1.1154 and the pound dipped 0.14 per cent to $1.3324.  Pesole also said he thought markets were positioning ahead of the Fed meeting, anticipating Chair Kevin Warsh will reiterate his commitment to fighting inflation, something that will reinforce the floor under the dollar. Several other factors are in the mix as well and a key gauge of Japan's service-sector inflation rose 3.7 per cent in September from a year earlier, data showed on Tuesday, a sign of increasing price pressures that will likely keep the central bank on track for further interest rate hikes. Also in Japan, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Tuesday the government stood ready to take decisive action in the currency market, reminding markets of Tokyo's willingness to intervene to prop up its currency.  TECH EARNINGS IMPACT The broader market story will also be tested by a number of corporate earnings this week including from AI hyperscalers Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon.com. The yen was among the best-performing major currencies last week, strengthening around 0.75 per cent on the dollar, its most since early September, as AI jitters in the equity market spurred a rush into the currency. Meanwhile, the euro was on track to be the worst-performing developed market currency in October, down 1.5 per cent on the dollar, bruised by high energy costs, and the volatility in French government bonds and worries about France's fiscal position. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Bank of Canada also announce their policy decisions on Wednesday, with both expected to raise interest rates. The RBNZ meets on Wednesday, and the New Zealand dollar was outperforming ahead of that, up 0.1 per cent on the dollar on Tuesday at $0.5687.  The Canadian dollar was steady at $1.4021 to its US counterpart.

Source: Reuters

Oct 27 : European digital privacy advocacy group noyb filed five complaints against Scale AI in France, Italy, the Netherlands and Austria on Tuesday, alleging it illegally monitored freelance workers who produce training data for AI models. The complaints target Outlier, a platform on which more than 900,000 freelancers perform various tasks that are recorded to create AI training data for clients such as Meta, OpenAI and Google. Meta owns 49 per cent of Scale AI. Noyb is asking regulators to fine Scale AI and to examine how the platform assigns tasks. "You don't work when you want," said Thomas Le Bonniec, who spent two years studying the platform for Paris-based research collective DiPLab. "You work when the platform wants you to and there are tasks available."

The complaints seen by Reuters said up to 19 trackers follow workers while they work, including recording keystrokes and mouse movements every few seconds. Outlier also uses game-like mechanisms, and bonuses are a key part of its incentive system, DiPLab found. ZURICH, Oct 27 : UBS will not allow the use of external AI models to execute actions on behalf of clients, CEO Sergio Ermotti said on Tuesday. Concerns that sophisticated AI agents could harm the financial system have risen within the banking industry. Major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents' access to customer accounts, people familiar with the matter have said. "You heard recently some banks are being exposed to potential misbehaviors of models in managing clients' accounts and shifting deposits and optimizing deposits," Ermotti told a science conference. "We are not allowing models to enter into the bank and do that." "When you talk about AI, the most important issue right now is to make sure that we don't get AI models that drive outcomes for clients in a black box," Ermotti said. UBS' integration of fallen rival Credit Suisse, which it acquired in 2023, forced it to slow its deployment of AI somewhat, but now the lender can put even more emphasis on technology, Ermotti added.  "I'm glad that we are almost over with the integration and therefore we can now put even more emphasis around technology and how we can help the bank become more effective and efficient."

BEIJING: China's industrial profits grew at a faster pace in September, though a deepening divergence across the economy weighed on business earnings. Profits at industrial firms rose 14.4 per cent from a year earlier last month, quickening from a 4.2 per cent increase in August, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Tuesday (Oct 27). Profits were up 15.5 per in the first nine months of this year, largely unchanged from the 15.7 per cent increase in the January-August period. The sectoral divide remained pronounced, with profits in the computer, communication and other electronic equipment manufacturing category more than doubling over the nine-month period, whereas profits in the furniture manufacturing sector fell by more than half, making it one of the worst performers. Also casting a shadow over the sustainability of profit growth, export-oriented firms are bracing for greater uncertainty as expanding trade surpluses stoke tensions with trading partners, particularly Europe.

"This suggests that domestic and external demand generated by the development of the AI supply chain has become a key force supporting industrial profits," he said. "Barring a major reversal in the global AI investment boom, industrial profits are expected to continue growing at a rapid pace." A stronger-than-expected 4.5 per cent expansion in third-quarter GDP put China within reach of its annual growth target of 4.5 per cent to 5.0 per cent, but disparities across different parts of the economy suggest the recovery remains unbalanced, with persistent weakness in some sectors continuing to erode corporate profitability. That pressure has become increasingly visible at the company level. Net profit growth at the world's largest electric vehicle battery maker, CATL, slowed sharply in the past quarter, as intense competition in the EV battery market squeezed margins at a time when China's auto sales were in a downturn. China will continue to leverage macroeconomic policies to support growth, expand domestic demand and optimize supply, said NBS statistician Yu Weining, underscoring a push to replace traditional growth drivers with new ones. TOKYO, Oct 27 : Moody's sees encouraging signs in Japan's return to sustained growth and stable inflation, but a key test will be whether that resilience can withstand future shocks, the rating agency's Japan sovereign analyst told Reuters on Tuesday. Moody's rates Japan at A1, its fifth-highest investment-grade rating, with a stable outlook, unchanged since its 2014 downgrade of Japan from Aa3. "We're starting to see what looks more like sustained growth and inflation expectations that are reasonably well anchored around 2 per cent," said Martin Petch, a vice president at the sovereign risk group of Moody's Ratings. "That's been something that's changed," Petch said in an interview, referring to a shift from decades of weak growth and chronically low inflation.

A key test, he added, is whether Japan can maintain growth and inflation stability through future economic shocks. "You can generally tell when growth has become sustained when the economy has dealt with a shock," Petch said, pointing out that Japan had coped well with recent energy-price shocks while the central bank keeps up efforts to normalise policy. LITTLE IMMEDIATE THREAT SEEN TO CREDIT PROFILE Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's food sales tax cut and ambitious spending plans rattled bond markets this year, but Petch suggested the measures have posed little immediate threat to Japan's credit profile. Their fiscal impact would depend on whether the government delivered on its pledge to offset the resulting revenue loss, he added. Although ministries have sought a record 143 trillion yen ($908 billion) in initial spending requests, Petch said the rise was relatively modest compared with combined initial and supplementary budgets. This reinforced Moody's view that there has been no meaningful departure from Japan's recent consolidation trend, he added. But uncertainties hover over the government's 370-trillion-yen public-private investment initiative, Petch said. These include the extent to which the private sector joins the initiative, and whether it can bring the productivity gains needed to offset Japan's demographic headwinds, he added. ($1=157.4700 yen)

SEOUL, Oct 27 : South Korea's semiconductor exports could fall by $50 billion to $100 billion compared with earlier forecasts if capital spending on artificial intelligence by major US technology firms slows next year, according to central bank data. In a written response submitted to lawmaker Ahn Do-geol, the Bank of Korea (BOK) modelled a "pessimistic scenario" to assess the economic fallout if US tech giants curb their aggressive infrastructure outlays. Under the scenario, a sudden export shortfall would shave approximately 0.4 per centage point off South Korea's gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate next year, by driving the country's current account surplus well below the central bank's initial projection of $430 billion for 2027. The scenario assumed a 10 per cent decline in Korean semiconductor unit prices.

SEOUL, Oct 27 : South Korean pop music agency JYP Entertainment's shares jumped 10 per cent on Tuesday after Korean media reported Japan's Nexroc Group and related firm SVCV Inc were planning to announce a tender offer to buy up to a 50 per cent stake in the company. The 50 per cent stake is worth about 700 billion won ($528.04 million) based on JYP's current market capitalisation. JYP said it has not received a tender offer. Nexroc Group was not immediately available to comment. JYP Entertainment, founded by South Korean singer-songwriter and producer Park Jin-young (J.Y. Park), is one of South Korea’s leading K-pop entertainment companies, with its main artists including popular K-pop groups such as TWICE, Stray Kids, ITZY and DAY6.

NEW DELHI, Oct 27 : Oil prices turned positive on Tuesday after a fall of about 1 per cent, earlier in the session, as the chance of talks in Tehran eased fears of a broader Middle East supply shock, while renewed Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia highlighted persistent risks. Brent crude futures was up 40 cents, or 0.4 per cent, at $116.24 a barrel by 0718 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude was up 30 cents, or 0.3 per cent, at $102.07. Both fell 1 per cent earlier in the session. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks with Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday aimed at easing tension in the Middle East. The four countries agreed to continue talks with a view to strengthening cooperation in peace and security, Iranian state media said.

"Prices remain elevated amid persistent geopolitical uncertainties," said Sugandha Sachdeva, founder of SS WealthStreet, a New Delhi-based research firm, adding that some profit taking earlier in the session was fuelled by hopes of a breakthrough in talks between the US and Iran, she said. Last week, Brent prices surged to more than $117 a barrel, the highest since April, after a wave of Iranian attacks on tankers around the Strait of Hormuz. Brent prices touched $117 on Monday as well. Scope for peace looked fragile, however, with renewed attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on key producer Saudi Arabia. October has been the worst month for attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and nearby waterways, data from a Washington-based think tank shows, among worldwide maritime security incidents it has tracked since 2017. The war rippling across the Middle East has brought into focus the narrow waterway of the Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of global energy supplies before the conflict erupted in February. The oil market is vulnerable with stress across areas such as supply, logistics, inventories and refining, ANZ Research said in a note. Gulf crude exports fell for a fourth straight week and flows through the Strait of Hormuz were just about 60 per cent of their normal level, while global distillate inventories held nearly 5 per cent below their five-year average, it added.

TOKYO: Japan's core consumer price index, which strips out one-off factors, rose in September at the fastest annual pace in three years, data showed on Tuesday (Oct 27), a sign of broadening price pressures that cement the case for further interest rate hikes. The data comes ahead of the Bank of Japan's two-day policy meeting that ends on Friday, when the central bank is set to keep interest rates steady at 1.25 per cent but signal its readiness to keep raising borrowing costs on mounting risks of inflation. The index, which excludes "institutional factors" such as education and energy-related subsidies, jumped 3.2 per cent in September from a year earlier, BOJ data showed, accelerating from a rise of 2.6 per cent in August. The index rise is the biggest year-on-year since October 2023.

The index is compiled by the BOJ to better gauge underlying inflation, or price moves driven by domestic demand that strips out the effect of government subsidies and other one-off steps. It is different from the government's core consumer price index, which excludes volatile fresh food costs but does not strip out the impact of subsides and other government steps. Separate data from the BOJ earlier on Tuesday showed a key gauge of service-sector inflation rose 3.7 per cent in September from a year earlier, suggesting that companies are passing on rising labour costs to service-related prices. "The data shows companies are passing on prices at the business-to-business level reflecting the strong outcome of this year's wage negotiations," said Kenichiro Ahara, an economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute. The annual rise in the services producer price index, which tracks the prices companies charge each other for services, followed a revised 3.5 per cent gain in August. A jump of 97.7 per cent in ocean freight transport costs was among key drivers of the increase, as the weak yen and Middle East conflict boosted the cost of importing fuel, the data showed. Still, prices of labour-incentive sectors continued to rise steadily in a sign of broadening price pressures, analysts said. The BOJ has said it focuses on underlying inflation in deciding the pace and timing of future interest rate hikes.

Source: Reuters/ec
